client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately because my final exams are coming up next month, and I just can't seem to shake this constant dread about it. Last semester I did really badly in chemistry, and now every time I sit down to study, I just freeze up and can't focus. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because at the end of the day I still have to actually pass these exams.
therapist: It makes complete sense that last semester's experience left a mark — your mind is trying to protect you from feeling that pain again, even if freezing up ends up working against you. You're right that talking won't take the exams for you, but it can help us loosen the grip that dread has on you so you can actually access the knowledge you have. I'm curious — when you sit down to study and that freeze hits, what's the very first thought that tends to run through your mind?

client: The first thought that usually hits me is something like, "What's the point, you're just going to fail again anyway." It's like this voice in my head that immediately reminds me of how badly I did last time, and then I just feel this heavy, sick feeling in my stomach and I can't move forward. I end up just staring at my notes or scrolling on my phone instead of actually doing anything.
therapist: That thought — "what's the point, you're just going to fail again anyway" — is a really powerful example of what we call an automatic thought, and it's worth noticing that it's presenting itself as a fact when it's actually a prediction your mind is making based on one past experience. That heavy, sick feeling and the freezing up make total sense as a response, because your brain has learned to associate studying with that pain. I'd gently invite you to consider — is there any evidence from your life, even outside of chemistry, that contradicts the idea that trying leads nowhere?

client: I mean, I guess there are other things I've done okay at — like I actually improved a lot in my English class after struggling at the start of the year. But it feels different with chemistry, like that subject has this specific power over me that other things don't, so I'm not sure those examples really count. It's hard to hold onto those other successes when the chemistry failure feels so much louder in my head.
therapist: You just did something really important — you found real evidence that you *can* struggle and then improve, even if your mind is trying to dismiss it as "not counting." It's so common for our brains to turn up the volume on painful experiences and mute the successes, but that doesn't make the English class improvement any less real or relevant. What do you think it was about that situation that allowed you to turn things around, and could any of that apply here?

client: In English, I think it helped that I asked my teacher for feedback early on and actually understood what I was doing wrong, so I had something concrete to fix. But with chemistry, the material itself just feels like a foreign language to me, and I'm not sure getting feedback will help if I fundamentally don't understand the concepts. I guess I could try talking to my professor, but honestly the idea of going to office hours and admitting how lost I am feels really embarrassing.
therapist: You've actually just uncovered your own strategy — early feedback was the key that unlocked improvement in English, and part of you already knows that's worth trying again here. That embarrassment about going to office hours is really understandable, but it's worth examining whether your professor is actually likely to judge you, or whether that's another prediction your mind is making to keep you "safe." What do you imagine the worst realistic outcome of going to office hours actually looks like, versus what might happen if you don't go at all?

client: I guess the worst realistic outcome is that my professor thinks I'm unprepared or not serious, and that feels humiliating even just imagining it. But if I don't go at all, I'll probably just keep freezing up and actually fail, which is what I'm terrified of in the first place. I can see the logic there, but knowing something makes sense and actually being able to make myself do it feel like two completely different things.
therapist: You've just shown really clear-eyed thinking there — you can see that the embarrassment of office hours is temporary and survivable, while avoiding it risks the very outcome you're most afraid of. And you're absolutely right that insight and action are different things, which is why instead of telling yourself "go to office hours," it might help to make it as small and low-stakes as possible — like just sending your professor one specific question by email first to ease into the connection. What would feel like the tiniest possible step you could actually see yourself taking in the next day or two?

client: Maybe I could look through my notes tonight and find one specific thing I genuinely don't understand, and then draft an email to my professor about just that one thing. But I'm already worried that even writing the email will take forever because I'll overthink every word and end up not sending it. I do that a lot — I start something small and then it snowballs into this whole production in my head and I just abandon it.
therapist: That's a really honest and self-aware observation — you've noticed a pattern where perfectionism sneaks in and turns a small step into an overwhelming production, which ends up protecting you from the very risk of being judged but also keeps you stuck. What if the email didn't have to be perfect, and you gave yourself a rule like "it only needs to be three sentences and sent within 10 minutes of drafting, typos and all"? What do you think would happen if you let it be a little messy and sent it anyway?

client: Honestly, the idea of sending something with typos or that isn't perfectly worded makes me cringe just thinking about it, because I'd probably spend the whole day after worrying about what my professor thought of me for sending a messy email. I think what would actually happen is I'd send it and then immediately regret it and feel anxious waiting for the reply. But I guess that anxiety would at least be about something real I actually did, instead of just this vague dread I'm carrying around right now.
therapist: That last thing you said is really profound — you recognized that action-based anxiety is actually a step forward from the paralyzed, vague dread you're living in right now, because it means you're in the game rather than on the sidelines. And the worry about your professor judging a slightly imperfect email is worth gently challenging — most professors see a student reaching out for help as a sign of seriousness, not the opposite. If a close friend sent you a slightly imperfect email asking for help, what would you actually think of them?

client: If a friend sent me a messy email asking for help, I'd honestly just think they were brave for reaching out and I'd want to help them. It's kind of uncomfortable to realize I'd never judge them the way I'm assuming my professor would judge me. I don't know why it's so easy to be kind to other people but when it comes to myself, that same logic just doesn't seem to stick.
therapist: You've just stumbled onto something really central — that gap between how compassionately you treat others and how harshly you treat yourself is something so many people struggle with, and simply noticing it is genuinely meaningful progress. That kindness you'd extend to a friend isn't a different logic, it's actually the *truer* logic, and you're capable of it — it's just a matter of slowly learning to include yourself in that circle of compassion. What do you think it would feel like to try speaking to yourself the way you'd speak to that friend, even just for the next few hours tonight as you look through your notes?

client: I want to say it would feel relieving, but honestly my first instinct is that it would just feel fake, like I'd be saying nice things to myself that I don't actually believe. I think I'd start with "it's okay that you don't understand this yet" and then immediately a part of me would shoot back with "no it's not, exams are in a month." I'm not sure how you actually make that kinder voice feel real instead of just like something you're performing.
therapist: That feeling of it being "fake" is actually really normal at the start — self-compassion often does feel like a performance before it feels genuine, because that kinder voice is like a muscle you haven't had much practice using yet. And that critical voice shooting back isn't wrong that exams matter, but notice it's treating urgency and self-kindness as opposites, when actually being kinder to yourself is likely what will help you *function* better over the next month. What if "it's okay you don't understand this yet" and "exams are in a month" could both be true at the same time — does that feel possible, even slightly?

client: When you put it that way, I can sort of see that both things could be true at the same time, like they don't actually cancel each other out. It's just that my brain seems really trained to think that being hard on myself is what keeps me motivated, and if I ease up even a little, I'll somehow stop caring and fall apart completely. I guess I'm scared that self-compassion is just another word for giving myself an excuse to not try hard enough.
therapist: That fear makes so much sense, but it's worth examining whether being hard on yourself has actually been producing the motivation you're hoping for — because from what you've described, the harshness seems to be leading to freezing, scrolling, and dread rather than focused studying. Research actually suggests the opposite of what your brain is predicting: self-compassion tends to increase resilience and effort because you're not spending so much energy just surviving your own inner critic. Looking back honestly, has the harsh voice ever actually helped you perform better, or has it mostly just made you feel worse?
